```{r, include = FALSE}
# Evaluated wherever a tier runs; where the system refuses writable and
# executable memory, nothing can be compiled, and the code is shown only.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = zumir::zumir_tier() != "none"
)
```

Making R code fast usually means rewriting it in C or C++ and installing a
toolchain: Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, `gcc`
elsewhere. Locked-down machines, Shiny servers and slim containers often
have none. zumir vendors MIR, a small JIT compiler, so a numeric R function,
or a short C function, can be compiled to native code from R with nothing
else installed.

```{r setup}
library(zumir)
```

## Compile an R function

`mir_compile()` takes a numeric R function and compiles it to native code.
The result has the same arguments and returns exactly what the R function
returns. It accepts doubles, loops over indices, conditions and the usual
maths; anything else is refused with the construct named. [What
`mir_compile()` accepts](mir-compile.html) lists the subset, and every
place it errors where R would answer differently.

```{r}
csum_r <- function(x) {
  y <- numeric(length(x))
  acc <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    acc <- acc + x[i]
    y[i] <- acc
  }
  y
}
csum <- mir_compile(csum_r)

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
csum(x)
identical(csum(x), csum_r(x))
```

The compiled loop runs far faster than the R loop, and close to R's own
`cumsum()`, which is written in C. Timings vary by machine.

```{r, eval = zumir::zumir_tier() != "none" && requireNamespace("bench", quietly = TRUE)}
x <- rnorm(1e6)
bench::mark(csum_r(x), csum(x), cumsum(x), min_iterations = 10)[, 1:5]
```

So `mir_compile()` pays off for a loop that R has no built-in for. Examples
are a recurrence, where each step needs the one before it, a loop that stops
early, and one pass that does what several vectorised calls would do. Where
R already has a built-in, such as `cumsum()`, `sum()` or vectorised
arithmetic, use the built-in. It is already compiled C, and the compiled
loop will not beat it. Compile once and call the result many times, because
compiling takes time too.

## Compile a C function

`cfunction()` takes the source of one C function and returns an R function
that calls it. The source defines one non-`static` function; `static`
helpers beside it are fine. Arguments named in `out` are allocated for you
and returned, and your own vectors are never changed. Lengths come from the
`int` argument you name.

```{r}
sq <- cfunction("
  void sq(int n, const double *x, double *y) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) y[i] = x[i] * x[i];
  }", out = "y", n = "n")

sq(x = c(1, 2, 3))
```

The cumulative sum from above, written in C, comes close to `cumsum()`. It
is a little faster than the compiled R loop, which also does what R does on
every step, such as checking for an interrupt.

```{r, eval = zumir::zumir_tier() != "none" && requireNamespace("bench", quietly = TRUE)}
csum_c <- cfunction("
  void csum_c(int n, const double *x, double *y) {
    double acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      acc += x[i];
      y[i] = acc;
    }
  }", out = "y", n = "n")

x <- rnorm(1e6)
bench::mark(csum(x), csum_c(x = x), cumsum(x), min_iterations = 10)[, 1:5]
```

## Return a value

A function that returns `int` or `double` gives that value back directly.

```{r}
dot <- cfunction("
  double dot(int n, const double *x, const double *y) {
    double s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += x[i] * y[i];
    return s;
  }", n = "n")

dot(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(4, 5, 6))
```

Arguments can be `int`, `double`, `const int *`, `const double *`, `int *`
and `double *`. The source may use the C maths library and a few memory and
string functions, but it can't include system headers or call R's API.

## Write MIR directly

`mir_function()` takes MIR's textual IR instead of C. It is useful for
tests, for learning MIR, and for checking a lowering by hand.

```{r}
f <- mir_function("
  m: module
     export add
  add: func d, d:a, d:b
     local d:r
     dadd r, a, b
     ret r
     endfunc
     endmodule", "add")

f(1, 2)
```

## Native code or the interpreter

zumir checks generated code when it loads. If that check fails, it falls
back to MIR's interpreter: results are the same, only slower. Where MIR
has no code generator for the CPU, or the system refuses memory that is
both writable and executable, no tier runs and nothing can be compiled.
`zumir_tier()` says which tier this session uses, and `zumir_info()` says
why. You can also ask for the interpreter yourself.

```{r}
zumir_tier()
zumir_info()

csum_interp <- mir_compile(csum_r, tier = "interp")
```
